transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-10
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Tom (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood ML), Carlos (Nimbus ML Platform), Meera (Nimbus Head of ML), James (Nimbus Infra), Sofia (Nimbus DS)

Summary (auto-gen - may be rough):
Quick review of INT8 vs FP8 quant experiments; INT8 gives ~2.3x token throughput and ~45% memory reduction vs FP16 baseline; FP8 shows similar throughput to INT8 with slightly better quality on a few prompt classes; identified 3 prompt families with regressions; agreed on longer 48h production-like benchmark and security/VPC follow-up.

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check 	6 can folks see my screen? I have slides and the benchmark spreadsheet linked in the calendar invite.
[00:08] Carlos: Yep, all good.
[00:10] Tom: Cool. I'll start with the perf summary then Priya will go through quality.
[00:15] Tom: So, to recap the last run 	6 we did three main configs: FP16 baseline, INT8 with our symmetric per-channel recipe, and FP8 (we called it F-P-eight in the run, sorry for the naming). The headline numbers: INT8 gave ~2.3x tokens/s vs FP16 and reduced GPU memory by ~45%. FP8 had similar throughput to INT8 on our A100 runs but used slightly less memory in some cases.
[00:40] Meera: When you say 2.3x, is that end-to-end latency or just token generation? Our P95 SLO is for end-to-end request latency.
[00:47] Tom: Good call 	6 that's token throughput in steady-state batching. End-to-end P95 for small single-turn requests improved by about 30% on INT8 because batching efficiency matters. For large context sessions (long KV cache use) FP8 sometimes keeps KV memory lower and avoids some evictions, so P95 was comparable or slightly better in FP8 for long sessions.
[01:15] James: Quick infra question 	6 did you change KV cache handling or was it identical across runs? We saw some weird swap activity last week.
[01:22] Tom: We kept KV logic identical; same cache policy. There is a small change where quantized weights reduce total GPU memory so less chance of kernel OOM and fewer cache spills. But if your deployment pins sequence length high, the savings shift more to KV allocated. We noted some swap on the 80k-context run 	6 could be our staging host.
[01:45] Priya: Okay quality 	6 we ran the standard eval set (1000 prompts) and also the customer-specific prompt bank (Nimbus-probes-v3, ~420 prompts). Overall aggregate accuracy drop on INT8 vs FP16 was 0.8% absolute on our main metric (answer-exactness), FP8 was ~0.5% drop. However, there are 3 prompt families where INT8 dropped 4-6% 	6 these are largely math-heavy deterministic prompts and a few with date normalization.
[02:20] Sofia: Can you show an example of a regression?
[02:23] Priya: Sure 	6 example: prompt asking for step-by-step calculation of compound interest. FP16 and FP8 handled it fine; INT8 occasionally produced swapped digits or rounding errors. We attached diffs in the sheet under "per-example-diffs".
[02:45] Carlos: Hmm. For us math correctness is important for our clinical billing predictions 	6 4-6% is risky. Can we mitigate?
[02:52] Priya: Options 	6 1) mixed-precision for the math head (keep key layers at FP16), 2) selective restoration: run the few problematic prompt families routed to FP16 or FP8, 3) quantization-aware fine-tuning on a small dataset focusing on those prompts.
[03:15] Meera: How heavy is the mixed-precision route in terms of throughput hit?
[03:20] Tom: In our tests, keeping the final MLP layers at FP16 and quantizing attention layers to INT8 caused throughput to drop to ~1.9x vs baseline 	6 so still much faster than FP16. Memory savings were slightly lower but still ~35% reduction.
[03:40] James: And operational complexity? If we run mixed-precision we need to ensure kernel combos are supported on our stack. We run a slightly older CUDA/runtime.
[03:50] Tom: Yes 	6 that's a compatibility check. We did see that older driver combos had some kernel fallbacks causing minor latency jitter. We'll include a compatibility matrix with the logs.
[04:05] Aisha: We put a link to the benchmark sheet in the chat 	6 "https://redwood-internal.sheets/nimbus-quant-bench" 	6 that has the per-run configs and per-prompt diffs.
[04:18] Carlos: Got it. I skimmed it earlier, but we'll review the diffs in detail.
[04:22] Priya: One more note 	6 FP8 runs were unstable on one of our small-instance configs (T4-like). On A100 FP8 was fine. So FP8 seems more sensitive to kernel/driver; INT8 is generally more robust.
[04:40] Meera: For security/compliance, we need to confirm encryption/KMS flow is not impacted by quantization 	6 I know it's orthogonal but wanted to flag. James will lead that.
[04:49] James: Yeah, I'll coordinate. From infra side we need to test with our VPC peering and HSM KMS; expect no functional change but want to validate artifacts/logs aren't leaking precision info or metadata.
[05:05] Aisha: Good call. We'll make sure the exported logs redact keys and include the KMS handshake trace.
[05:12] Tom: Back to perf 	6 we also ran stress throughput (batching up to 256 tokens/batch). INT8 maintains linear scaling until ~180 batch size then a tiny kernel saturation. FP8 sometimes pushes a bit higher before network becomes the bottleneck.
[05:35] Sofia: Any differences in sampling quality 	6 hallucinations or verbosity 	6 between INT8/FP8?
[05:40] Priya: Not major. We measured hallucination rate on the hallucination-suite (50 prompts) 	6 INT8 +0.3% vs FP16, FP8 +0.15%. Those are within noise but the math-family regressions dominate concern.
[05:58] Carlos: What about tokenization edge cases 	6 hyphenated clinical codes?
[06:02] Priya: We flagged a couple; they were more generation formatting differences rather than tokenization failures. We'll include examples.
[06:10] Tom: We're recommending short-term path A: run a targeted quant-aware fine-tune on the math/date families with INT8 profile and re-eval; path B: enable routing so those prompts go to FP16 or FP8; path C: deploy mixed-precision recipe. We prefer A+B in combination.
[06:30] Meera: Cost-wise, how does INT8 dedicated capacity pricing compare? Aisha?
[06:34] Aisha: We ran rough numbers 	6 INT8 with dedicated reserved capacity yields ~40-50% lower per-token cost vs FP16 hosted. For dedicated, the delta depends on utilization; I'll send a modeled pricing sheet.
[06:48] Carlos: Important: we need deterministic reproducibility for audits. Does quantization change determinism?
[06:54] Tom: Quantization can introduce nondeterminism if using non-deterministic kernels or fused ops. We can enforce deterministic kernels but may impact perf. We'll call out which kernels are deterministic in the compatibility matrix.
[07:12] James: Also want to log model version + quant recipe hashes into audit logs 	6 not just the model name.
[07:17] Aisha: Agreed 	6 Redwood can include recipe hashes in rollout metadata.
[07:22] Meera: Next steps and responsibilities?
[07:25] Aisha: I'll summarize: Redwood provides full perf logs + kernel compatibility matrix (Tom). Tom will also attach per-example diffs and the suggested mixed-precision recipe. Priya will prep the small fine-tune recipe focusing on the 3 reg families. Nimbus runs the 48h benchmark on their staging cluster and shares traces. James and Redwood schedule KMS/VPC deep-dive. Pricing sheet from me.
[07:44] Carlos: Sounds good. One more ask 	6 can we get a quick canary config that routes only flagged prompts to FP16 at inference time? We want to test in production with low % of traffic.
[07:53] Tom: Yes, we can provide a routing policy snippet and SDK example. We'll aim to have a canary config ready in 3 business days.
[08:02] Sofia: For the fine-tune, how much data do you expect?
[08:05] Priya: For targeted quant-aware fine-tune, usually 2-5k focused examples suffice. We can start with 2k from Nimbus-probes and see.
[08:15] Meera: Good. If the regressions are fixed with fine-tune then we can move forward with INT8. If not, we evaluate FP8 or mixed.
[08:23] Aisha: Ok closing 	6 we'll follow up in email with the artifacts. Next sync: same time next week, unless we need an earlier infra deep-dive.
[08:31] Carlos: Thanks all.
[08:33] Aisha: Thanks, bye.
